analysis.one_liner: Lets federal courts use evidence from searches police reasonably believed were legal, weakening the exclusionary rule.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 289-142 on February 8, 1995, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, federal courts throw out evidence gathered through an illegal search — the main penalty for police who violate the Fourth Amendment. This bill would let courts admit that evidence anyway whenever police had an 'objectively reasonable' belief the search was legal, and it would bar judges from suppressing evidence obtained in violation of statutes or agency rules. It would make the presence of a warrant strong proof the search was valid. It passed the House but never got a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal prosecutors and law enforcement, who would gain a new weapon: evidence from illegal or rule-breaking searches could be used at trial as long as the officer's mistake was reasonable. Cases that today collapse because of a botched search would survive.

how_it_helps.text: Courts could no longer exclude evidence from a search or seizure that was carried out under circumstances supporting an objectively reasonable belief it complied with the Fourth Amendment [S2][S4].
The fact that a search was done under a warrant would be prima facie evidence that the search was valid, shifting the burden onto the person challenging it [S2][S4].

Evidence obtained in violation of a statute, administrative rule, or procedural rule could no longer be suppressed unless a statute or Supreme Court rule expressly authorizes exclusion, and an objectively reasonable mistake about the law would also bar suppression [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Criminal defendants first — including people charged but not guilty — who would lose the chief remedy for illegal searches. More broadly, everyone loses the deterrent: if evidence from an unlawful search still gets used, police have little reason not to search aggressively.

drawbacks.text: The bill would largely remove the main consequence for illegal searches, since an officer's objectively reasonable mistake would no longer matter — critics viewed it as effectively repealing the exclusionary rule for federal cases [S2][S4].
It would bar suppression of evidence obtained through violations of statutes and regulations, so a police search that broke a privacy law could still be used at trial [S4].
It makes a warrant prima facie proof of validity, which shifts the practical burden of proving an unlawful search onto the person whose home was searched [S2][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argued the exclusionary rule lets guilty people go free over honest police mistakes that don't deter future misconduct, and courts had already carved out good-faith exceptions for warrant errors. The bill goes much further than those exceptions: it would leave almost no remedy for unlawful searches except an unreasonably bad one, and Congress has no authority to override the Constitution — so its constitutionality was doubtful and its main real-world effect would be weakening protection against intrusive government searches.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 289-142, but the Senate referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which never brought it up, and it died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced January 25, 1995, and reported by the House Judiciary Committee on a 19-14 vote within days [S1][S6].
The House passed it 289-142 on February 8, 1995, with Republicans 220-7 in favor and Democrats 69-134 against [S7][S6].
The Senate received the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee on February 9, 1995; no further action was taken [S6][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died in committee, the existing exclusionary rule stayed intact — criminal defendants and everyone's protection against unlawful searches were preserved, and prosecutors did not get the new evidentiary tool.

for.name: Rep. Bill McCollum
for.role: House sponsor; chair of the Judiciary crime subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and managed its House floor passage

for.name: House Judiciary Committee majority
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill on a 19-14 vote one day after markup

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on February 9, 1995, letting it die

sides.party_line_note: Republicans backed it nearly unanimously (220-7) while Democrats opposed it nearly two to one (69 yes, 134 no), so passage depended on 69 crossover Democratic votes.

industries.industry: Federal prosecutors and law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill would let prosecutors use evidence from unlawful or rule-breaking searches whenever the officer's mistake was reasonable, removing the main deterrent to illegal searches. Ordinary people would bear the cost through weakened Fourth Amendment protection. Notably, the bill carves out ATF and IRS searches, which would remain subject to full exclusion [S4].
